title: Bridges That Last
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Every bridge must deal with two forces. Compression squeezes a material together, and tension pulls it apart. Engineers choose the shape of a bridge according to how it shares these forces between its parts. Over the centuries, four main designs have emerged, each suited to a different distance, and each solving the problem in its own way. The choice is never only technical: the width of the river, the nature of the ground and the budget all play a part.

The simplest design is the beam bridge, which is a horizontal beam resting on supports at each end. A fallen tree across a stream is the earliest example. When a load crosses the beam, the top of the beam is squeezed and the bottom is stretched, so beams are strong only over short distances. The longest rarely exceed 250 metres, and to cross a wide river they need many piers, which can be expensive to build and may block the flow of water.

The arch turns the downward weight of the bridge into compression, which stone handles very well. The Romans built arches that are still standing after two thousand years. The curved shape pushes outwards at its base, so an arch needs strong abutments, heavy blocks of stone or concrete at each end, to stop it from spreading. Arches are rarely used for spans longer than about 500 metres, but in the right valley, with solid rock on both sides, they are hard to beat for both beauty and strength.

The suspension bridge hangs the road from huge cables that are draped over tall towers and anchored firmly at both ends. The cables carry the load in tension, and steel wire, which is strong when pulled, is the ideal material. The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan has a central span of 1,991 metres. Suspension bridges can move in the wind, however. In 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the United States twisted itself apart in a wind of only sixty-four kilometres per hour, and since then designers have tested models in wind tunnels.

The cable-stayed bridge looks similar but works differently. Its cables run straight from the towers to the road, in a pattern like the strings of a harp or the spokes of a fan, and there is no need for the enormous anchorages at the ends. This design is cheaper and faster to build over medium distances of between 200 and 1,000 metres, and it has become popular since the 1980s. The Russky Bridge in Vladivostok, with a span of 1,104 metres, is the longest of its kind in the world.

Building a bridge is only the beginning. Steel rusts, concrete cracks, and the number of vehicles often grows far beyond what the designers expected. Many countries now fit sensors to their bridges to measure movement and strain. According to the engineer Dr Hana Petrova, the data from sensors can warn of problems years before they can be seen by the eye, and a repair done early may cost one tenth of a repair done late. Even so, repairs are often delayed, because a bridge that still stands seems to be in no danger.

Engineers are also trying new materials. Fibre-reinforced plastics, which are lighter than steel and do not rust, are already used for footbridges. Researchers have developed a self-healing concrete that contains bacteria; when a crack lets in water, the bacteria wake up and produce limestone that seals the gap. Designers may soon be able to build a bridge that repairs itself, and so lasts far longer than the hundred years that most bridges are expected to survive.
